solution:
A potentiometer is a device used for the accurate measurement of potential difference and emf, without drawing any current from the source being measured.
Construction: it consists of a long wire AB of length \(L\), resistance \(R\) and uniform cross-sectional area \(A\), stretched on a wooden board. A cell of emf \(\varepsilon\) with internal resistance \(r\), a key and (usually) a rheostat are connected across AB, so that a steady current flows through the wire and a uniform fall of potential is set up along it.
Because at the balance (null) point no current is drawn from the cell under test, a potentiometer behaves as an ideal voltmeter of infinite resistance.

Potential gradient is defined as the potential difference per unit length of the potentiometer wire.
If \(V_{AB}\) is the potential difference across a wire AB of length \(L\), the potential gradient is
\(K = \dfrac{V_{AB}}{L} = \dfrac{\varepsilon R}{L (R + r)}\)
Its SI unit is volt per metre (V/m). As long as \(\varepsilon\), \(R\), \(r\) and \(L\) stay constant, \(K\) is constant along the wire.

The jockey should only be TAPPED on the wire, never slid along it.
Sliding the jockey scrapes and rubs the wire, so the wire is no longer of uniform cross section along its length. The resistance per unit length then varies from place to place, the potential gradient along the wire stops being uniform, and the relation \(V \propto l\) — on which the whole instrument rests — fails.
Tapping is enough for the purpose, because the jockey is used only to detect whether a current flows through the central (galvanometer) branch.

Yes. Kirchhoff's laws hold for both AC and DC circuits.
The junction law is a statement of the conservation of electric charge and the loop law is a statement of the conservation of energy, and both conservation principles hold at every instant, whether the current is steady or varying.
For an alternating current the laws are applied to the INSTANTANEOUS values of the currents and voltages (for a sinusoidal steady state they may equivalently be applied to the phasors), and the algebraic sums must be taken with due regard to phase.

The value of the known resistance \(R\) is adjusted so that the null point falls in the middle one third of the wire, i.e. between 34 cm and 66 cm.
Reason: the unknown resistance is found from \(X = \dfrac{l_x}{l_R} R\), so the accuracy of \(X\) depends on the accuracy of BOTH measured lengths. Every length reading carries the same absolute uncertainty (the least count of the metre scale), so the PERCENTAGE error in a length is largest when that length is small. Keeping the null point near the middle makes \(l_x\) and \(l_R\) comparable, so the percentage errors in the two are both minimum and nearly the same, and the error in \(X\) is least.

Sources of error in a metre-bridge experiment (any two):
1. The cross section of the bridge wire may not be uniform, so its resistance per unit length is not constant.
2. The ends of the wire are soldered to the metallic strips, where a contact resistance develops which is not taken into account.
3. The measurements of \(l_x\) and \(l_R\) may not be accurate.
How they are minimized:
(i) \(R\) is so chosen that the null point lies in the middle one third of the wire (between 34 cm and 66 cm), which makes the percentage errors in \(l_x\) and \(l_R\) minimum and nearly equal.
(ii) The experiment is repeated after interchanging the positions of the unknown resistance \(X\) and the resistance box \(R\), and the mean is taken — this cancels the end (contact) resistances.
(iii) The jockey is tapped on the wire and not slid along it, so the wire is not scraped and stays uniform.

Potential gradient is the potential difference per unit length of the potentiometer wire, denoted by \(K\).
For a wire AB of length \(L\) and resistance \(R\) connected across a cell of emf \(\varepsilon\) and internal resistance \(r\), the current is \(I = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{R + r}\), so
\(V_{AB} = IR = \dfrac{\varepsilon R}{R + r}\)
\(K = \dfrac{V_{AB}}{L} = \dfrac{\varepsilon R}{L (R + r)}\)
How it is measured: a cell of KNOWN emf \(\varepsilon_s\) is balanced against the wire, and the balancing length \(l\) from the end A is measured with the metre scale. Since \(\varepsilon_s = K l\),
\(K = \dfrac{\varepsilon_s}{l}\)
(Equivalently, the potential difference \(V_{AB}\) across the whole wire is measured and divided by the length \(L\).) Once \(K\) is known, the potential difference between any two points on the wire a distance \(l\) apart is \(V = K l\).

From \(K = \dfrac{\varepsilon R}{L (R + r)}\), the potential gradient of the wire depends on:
1. the emf \(\varepsilon\) of the driving (auxiliary) cell,
2. the resistance \(R\) of the potentiometer wire,
3. the internal resistance \(r\) of the driving cell together with any series resistance such as the rheostat,
4. the length \(L\) of the potentiometer wire.
Equivalently, writing \(K = \dfrac{IR}{L}\) and \(R = \dfrac{\rho L}{A}\) gives \(K = \dfrac{I \rho}{A}\), so the gradient depends on the current \(I\) through the wire, the resistivity \(\rho\) of its material and its area of cross section \(A\) — but NOT on the length, once the current is fixed.

A voltmeter, however good, has a finite resistance and therefore draws some current from the cell. The reading it gives is the TERMINAL potential difference \(V = \varepsilon - I r\), which is always less than the emf; a voltmeter can never measure emf.
A potentiometer works on a null method: at the balance point the galvanometer shows no deflection, so NO current is drawn from the cell under test. With \(I = 0\) the terminal potential difference equals the emf itself, and the potentiometer behaves as an ideal voltmeter of infinite resistance.
It is also far more sensitive — a potential difference of the order of \(10^{-6}\) V can be measured with it, and its least count is much better than that of a voltmeter.
Hence a potentiometer is preferred over a voltmeter for measuring emf.

Uses of a potentiometer:
1. To compare the emfs of two cells — either by connecting the cells individually, or by the sum and difference method.
2. To determine the internal resistance of a cell.
3. As a voltage divider, to vary the output voltage of a supply continuously between zero and its maximum value.
4. As an audio control — sliding (fader) and rotary (knob) potentiometers are used in audio systems for loudness control, frequency attenuation and tone control.
5. As a sensor — if the slider is coupled to a moving part of a machine, a small displacement changes the output potential, which after amplification is calibrated in terms of the displacement.
6. For accurate measurement of a potential difference, and for measuring a very small potential difference (of the order of \(10^{-6}\) V).

Disadvantages (demerits) of a potentiometer:
1. It is not portable — it needs a long wire stretched on a board, an auxiliary battery, a rheostat and a galvanometer, so it is a laboratory instrument and cannot be carried about like a voltmeter.
2. Direct measurement of a potential difference or an emf is not possible. It gives only a comparison: a balancing length is measured and the result is obtained from the potential gradient, which itself has to be established first (for example with a cell of known emf).
3. It is therefore slower and less convenient than a voltmeter for a routine reading.

| Potentiometer | Voltmeter |
|---|---|
| Draws no current from the cell at the balance point, so it acts as an ideal voltmeter of infinite resistance. | Has a finite resistance and always draws some current from the cell. |
| Measures the emf of a cell as well as a potential difference. | Measures only the terminal potential difference \(V = \varepsilon - Ir\); it cannot measure emf. |
| Null (balance) method — the reading is a length, converted using the potential gradient. | Deflection method — the reading is taken directly off a calibrated scale. |
| Very sensitive; a potential difference of the order of \(10^{-6}\) V can be measured, so its least count is much better. | Much less sensitive; least count is comparatively poor. |
| Not portable, and no direct reading is possible. | Portable and gives a direct reading. |

The balancing length is fixed by \(\varepsilon = K l\), i.e. \(l = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{K}\), and the potential gradient is \(K = \dfrac{IR}{L}\), which is directly proportional to the current \(I\) through the potentiometer wire. The emf \(\varepsilon\) being balanced does not change.
(i) If the current is INCREASED, \(K\) increases, so \(l\) DECREASES — the point of zero deflection shifts towards the end A (the end at higher potential), i.e. the null point moves nearer to the start of the wire.
(ii) If the current is DECREASED, \(K\) decreases, so \(l\) INCREASES — the point of zero deflection shifts away from A, towards the end B.
If the current is reduced so far that \(K L < \varepsilon\), no balance point can be found anywhere on the wire.

Four resistances \(P\), \(Q\), \(R\) and \(S\) are connected to form a quadrilateral ABCD. A cell of emf \(\varepsilon\) with a key is connected between A and C (A at the higher potential) and a galvanometer of resistance \(G\) is connected between B and D.
When the key is closed the current \(I\) divides at A into \(I_1\) through \(P\) and \(I_2\) through \(S\); \(I_g\) flows through the galvanometer, so the currents through \(Q\) and \(R\) are \((I_1 - I_g)\) and \((I_2 + I_g)\).
\(I = I_1 + I_2\) --- (1)
Applying Kirchhoff's voltage law to the loop ABDA (clockwise):
\(-I_1 P - I_g G + I_2 S = 0\) --- (2)
Applying Kirchhoff's voltage law to the loop BCDB (clockwise):
\(-(I_1 - I_g) Q + (I_2 + I_g) R + I_g G = 0\) --- (3)
The bridge is said to be BALANCED when no current flows through the galvanometer, i.e. \(I_g = 0\). Putting \(I_g = 0\) in (2) and (3):
\(-I_1 P + I_2 S = 0\), so \(I_1 P = I_2 S\) --- (4)
\(-I_1 Q + I_2 R = 0\), so \(I_1 Q = I_2 R\) --- (5)
Dividing (4) by (5):
\(\dfrac{P}{Q} = \dfrac{S}{R}\)
This is the balancing condition of the Wheatstone bridge. If any three of the four resistances are known, the fourth can be found from it.

Construction: a metre bridge consists of a wire of uniform cross section, exactly one metre long, stretched along a metre scale on a wooden board. The ends of the wire are fixed below two L-shaped metallic strips, and a third strip between them leaves two gaps — the left gap and the right gap. The unknown resistance \(X\) is connected in the left gap and a resistance box \(R\) in the right gap. One terminal of a galvanometer is joined to the central strip C, the other terminal carries the jockey J. A cell \(\varepsilon\) with a key and a rheostat is connected across the ends A and B of the wire.
Working: a suitable resistance \(R\) is taken from the box, and the jockey is TAPPED at different points of the wire until the galvanometer shows no deflection. That point D is the null (balance) point.
Calculation: the metre bridge is a Wheatstone bridge in which the two lower arms are the two parts AD and DB of the wire. Let their lengths be \(l_x\) and \(l_R\) and their resistances \(R_{AD}\) and \(R_{DB}\). At balance,
\(\dfrac{X}{R} = \dfrac{R_{AD}}{R_{DB}}\)
Since the wire is uniform, of resistivity \(\rho\) and area of cross section \(A\),
\(R_{AD} = \dfrac{\rho l_x}{A}\) and \(R_{DB} = \dfrac{\rho l_R}{A}\)
\(\dfrac{X}{R} = \dfrac{\rho l_x / A}{\rho l_R / A} = \dfrac{l_x}{l_R}\)
\(\therefore X = \dfrac{l_x}{l_R} R\)
Knowing \(R\), \(l_x\) and \(l_R\), the unknown resistance \(X\) is determined. \(R\) is chosen so that the null point lies in the middle one third of the wire, and the reading is repeated with \(X\) and \(R\) interchanged, to reduce the error.

Kelvin's method determines the resistance \(G\) of a galvanometer using a metre bridge.
Circuit: the galvanometer whose resistance is to be found is connected in ONE gap of the metre bridge and a known resistance \(R\) (resistance box) in the other gap. Unlike the ordinary metre-bridge circuit, here the galvanometer itself is one arm of the bridge, and one of its terminals is joined to the central strip so that the jockey and the wire complete the network.
Working:
1. A suitable resistance is taken in the box and the current is sent round the circuit by closing the key. Without touching the jockey anywhere on the wire, the deflection in the galvanometer is observed.
2. The rheostat is adjusted to bring this deflection to about two thirds of the range.
3. The jockey is then tapped at different points of the wire, and the point of contact D is found at which the galvanometer shows NO CHANGE in its deflection.
4. Since the galvanometer shows the same deflection with or without the contact at D, no current flows through the branch containing D, so B and D are at the same potential — they are equipotential points, and the bridge is balanced.
5. The length of the bridge wire from D to the left end is measured. Let \(l_g\) be the length of the segment opposite to the galvanometer and \(l_r\) the length opposite to the resistance box, with \(l_g + l_r = 100\) cm.
Calculation: since the bridge is balanced,
\(\dfrac{G}{R} = \dfrac{R_{AD}}{R_{DC}}\) and \(\dfrac{R_{AD}}{R_{DC}} = \dfrac{l_g}{l_r}\)
\(\therefore \dfrac{G}{R} = \dfrac{l_g}{100 - l_g}\)
\(\therefore G = \left(\dfrac{l_g}{100 - l_g}\right) R\)
Using this formula the unknown resistance of the galvanometer is calculated.
Note the distinguishing feature of Kelvin's method: the balance point is the one at which the deflection does not CHANGE when the jockey touches the wire, not the one at which the deflection is zero.

Circuit: a potentiometer circuit is set up by connecting a battery of emf \(\varepsilon\), a key K and a rheostat across the wire AB, with A at the higher potential. The two cells whose emfs \(\varepsilon_1\) and \(\varepsilon_2\) are to be compared have their POSITIVE terminals joined together at the point A, and their negative terminals joined to the two extreme terminals of a two-way key \(K_1 K_2\). The central terminal of the two-way key is connected to a galvanometer, whose other end carries the jockey J.
Working:
Step 1: key K is closed, then \(K_1\) is closed and \(K_2\) is kept open, so the cell of emf \(\varepsilon_1\) alone is in the circuit. The jockey is tapped along AB until the galvanometer shows no deflection. Let \(l_1\) be the length of wire from A to this null point. Then
\(\varepsilon_1 = k\, l_1\)
where \(k\) is the potential gradient along the wire.
Step 2: \(K_1\) is now opened and \(K_2\) is closed, so the cell of emf \(\varepsilon_2\) comes into the circuit. The null point is found again; let its distance from A be \(l_2\). Then
\(\varepsilon_2 = k\, l_2\)
Comparison: dividing the two equations (\(k\) is the same in both, because the current through AB is not disturbed),
\(\dfrac{\varepsilon_1}{\varepsilon_2} = \dfrac{l_1}{l_2}\)
Thus the emfs of the two cells are compared. If either emf is known, the other can be determined.

This is the SUM AND DIFFERENCE method.
Sum mode: if the negative terminal of the first cell is joined to the positive terminal of the second, the two emfs add and the effective emf of the combination is \(\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2\).
Difference mode: if the two negative terminals (or the two positive terminals) are joined together, the emfs oppose and the effective emf is \(\varepsilon_1 - \varepsilon_2\) (taking \(\varepsilon_1 > \varepsilon_2\)). Note that this is NOT a parallel combination of cells.
Working: the circuit is connected with four keys \(K_1, K_2, K_3, K_4\) so that either mode can be selected.
Step 1: keys \(K_1\) and \(K_3\) are closed, putting the cells in the SUM mode. The null point is obtained with the jockey; let \(l_1\) be its distance from A. This length corresponds to \((\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2)\):
\(\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2 = k\, l_1\)
Step 2: \(K_1\) and \(K_3\) are opened and \(K_2\) and \(K_4\) are closed, putting the cells in the DIFFERENCE mode. The null point is obtained again at a distance \(l_2\) from A, corresponding to \((\varepsilon_1 - \varepsilon_2)\):
\(\varepsilon_1 - \varepsilon_2 = k\, l_2\)
Comparison: dividing,
\(\dfrac{\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2}{\varepsilon_1 - \varepsilon_2} = \dfrac{l_1}{l_2}\)
Applying componendo and dividendo,
\(\dfrac{\varepsilon_1}{\varepsilon_2} = \dfrac{l_1 + l_2}{l_1 - l_2}\)
Thus the emfs of the two cells are compared.

Circuit: the potentiometer wire AB is connected in series with a cell of emf \(\varepsilon\), a key \(K_1\) and a rheostat, with terminal A at the higher potential. The cell of emf \(\varepsilon_1\) whose internal resistance \(r\) is to be found is connected between A and the jockey J through a galvanometer G. A resistance box \(R\) is connected ACROSS this cell through a second key \(K_2\).
Step 1 — open circuit: \(K_1\) is closed and \(K_2\) is kept OPEN, so no current is drawn from the cell \(\varepsilon_1\). The null point is found; let \(l_1\) be its distance from A. This length corresponds to the EMF of the cell:
\(\varepsilon_1 = k\, l_1\) --- (1)
where \(k\) is the (constant) potential gradient of the wire.
Step 2 — closed circuit: both \(K_1\) and \(K_2\) are closed, so the cell now sends a current \(I\) through the resistance box \(R\). The null point is obtained again at a distance \(l_2\) from A. This length now corresponds to the TERMINAL potential difference \(V\) across the cell:
\(V = k\, l_2\) --- (2)
Derivation: from (1) and (2),
\(\dfrac{\varepsilon_1}{V} = \dfrac{k l_1}{k l_2} = \dfrac{l_1}{l_2}\)
For the loop containing the cell and the resistance box,
\(\varepsilon_1 = IR + Ir\) and \(V = IR\)
\(\therefore \dfrac{\varepsilon_1}{V} = \dfrac{IR + Ir}{IR} = \dfrac{R + r}{R} = \dfrac{l_1}{l_2}\)
\(\therefore \dfrac{r}{R} = \dfrac{l_1}{l_2} - 1\)
\(\therefore r = R \left(\dfrac{l_1}{l_2} - 1\right) = R \left(\dfrac{l_1 - l_2}{l_2}\right)\)
This is the required formula; \(R\), \(l_1\) and \(l_2\) are all measured, so \(r\) is determined.

Given: \(\varepsilon_1 = 4\) V, \(r_1 = 1\ \Omega\); \(\varepsilon_2 = 1\) V, \(r_2 = 1\ \Omega\); external resistance \(R = 2\ \Omega\).
The like poles are joined together, so the two cells are in parallel and their emfs act in the same sense.
Equivalent emf of the parallel combination:
\(\varepsilon_{eq} = \dfrac{\dfrac{\varepsilon_1}{r_1} + \dfrac{\varepsilon_2}{r_2}}{\dfrac{1}{r_1} + \dfrac{1}{r_2}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{4}{1} + \dfrac{1}{1}}{\dfrac{1}{1} + \dfrac{1}{1}} = \dfrac{5}{2} = 2.5\) V
Equivalent internal resistance:
\(r_{eq} = \dfrac{r_1 r_2}{r_1 + r_2} = \dfrac{1 \times 1}{1 + 1} = 0.5\ \Omega\)
Current through the external resistance:
\(I = \dfrac{\varepsilon_{eq}}{r_{eq} + R} = \dfrac{2.5}{0.5 + 2} = \dfrac{2.5}{2.5}\)
\(\therefore I = 1\) A

Given: \(\varepsilon_1 = 1.5\) V, \(r_1 = 1\ \Omega\); \(\varepsilon_2 = 2\) V, \(r_2 = 2\ \Omega\); external resistance \(R = 5\ \Omega\). The cells are in parallel and send current in the same direction.
Equivalent emf:
\(\varepsilon_{eq} = \dfrac{\dfrac{\varepsilon_1}{r_1} + \dfrac{\varepsilon_2}{r_2}}{\dfrac{1}{r_1} + \dfrac{1}{r_2}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{1.5}{1} + \dfrac{2}{2}}{\dfrac{1}{1} + \dfrac{1}{2}} = \dfrac{2.5}{1.5} = \dfrac{5}{3}\) V
Equivalent internal resistance:
\(r_{eq} = \dfrac{r_1 r_2}{r_1 + r_2} = \dfrac{1 \times 2}{1 + 2} = \dfrac{2}{3}\ \Omega\)
Current through the external resistance:
\(I = \dfrac{\varepsilon_{eq}}{r_{eq} + R} = \dfrac{5/3}{\dfrac{2}{3} + 5} = \dfrac{5/3}{17/3}\)
\(\therefore I = \dfrac{5}{17} \approx 0.294\) A

Given: voltmeter resistance \(R_V = 30\ \Omega\), emf \(\varepsilon = 2\) V, internal resistance \(r = 10\ \Omega\).
The voltmeter is connected across the cell, so the cell drives a current through the series combination of its own internal resistance and the voltmeter:
\(I = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{R_V + r} = \dfrac{2}{30 + 10} = \dfrac{2}{40} = 0.05\) A
The voltmeter reads the potential difference across itself, which is the TERMINAL potential difference of the cell:
\(V = I R_V = 0.05 \times 30\)
\(\therefore V = 1.5\) V
Note that this is less than the emf of 2 V, because the voltmeter draws current — which is exactly why a voltmeter cannot measure emf.

Given: three coils of \(10\ \Omega\), \(12\ \Omega\) and \(15\ \Omega\); \(\varepsilon = 4.1\) V.
Parallel combination of the three coils:
\(\dfrac{1}{R_p} = \dfrac{1}{10} + \dfrac{1}{12} + \dfrac{1}{15} = \dfrac{6 + 5 + 4}{60} = \dfrac{15}{60} = \dfrac{1}{4}\)
\(R_p = 4\ \Omega\)
Series combination of three coils of the same resistances:
\(R_s = 10 + 12 + 15 = 37\ \Omega\)
The two combinations are joined in series, so the total resistance of the circuit is
\(R = R_p + R_s = 4 + 37 = 41\ \Omega\)
Current through the circuit:
\(I = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{R} = \dfrac{4.1}{41}\)
\(\therefore I = 0.1\) A

Given: length of the potentiometer wire \(L = 1.5\) m \(= 150\) cm, resistance of the wire \(R = 10\ \Omega\), emf of the driving cell \(\varepsilon = 4\) V, internal resistance \(r = 5\ \Omega\).
Current through the wire:
\(I = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{R + r} = \dfrac{4}{10 + 5} = \dfrac{4}{15}\) A
Potential difference across the whole wire:
\(V_{AB} = I R = \dfrac{4}{15} \times 10 = \dfrac{8}{3} = 2.667\) V
Potential drop per centimetre (the potential gradient):
\(K = \dfrac{V_{AB}}{L} = \dfrac{2.667}{150}\)
\(\therefore K = 0.01778 \approx 0.0178\) V/cm
(Equivalently \(1.778\) V/m.)

Given: balancing length in the sum mode \(l_1 = 2.7\) m, in the difference mode \(l_2 = 0.3\) m.
In the sum mode the effective emf is \(\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2 = k\, l_1\); in the difference mode it is \(\varepsilon_1 - \varepsilon_2 = k\, l_2\).
Dividing (the potential gradient \(k\) is the same in both):
\(\dfrac{\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2}{\varepsilon_1 - \varepsilon_2} = \dfrac{l_1}{l_2} = \dfrac{2.7}{0.3} = 9\)
Applying componendo and dividendo,
\(\dfrac{\varepsilon_1}{\varepsilon_2} = \dfrac{l_1 + l_2}{l_1 - l_2} = \dfrac{2.7 + 0.3}{2.7 - 0.3} = \dfrac{3.0}{2.4} = \dfrac{5}{4}\)
\(\therefore \dfrac{\varepsilon_1}{\varepsilon_2} = 1.25\)
The emf of the first cell is 1.25 times that of the second.

Given: open-circuit balancing length \(l_1 = 120\) cm; the balancing length is reduced by 20 cm when the cell is shunted, so the closed-circuit balancing length is \(l_2 = 120 - 20 = 100\) cm; shunt (external) resistance \(R = 10\ \Omega\).
Internal resistance of the cell:
\(r = R \left(\dfrac{l_1 - l_2}{l_2}\right) = 10 \times \left(\dfrac{120 - 100}{100}\right) = 10 \times \dfrac{20}{100}\)
\(\therefore r = 2\ \Omega\)

Given: potential gradient \(K = 5 \times 10^{-3}\) V/m; balancing length \(l = 216\) cm \(= 2.16\) m.
At the balance point no current is drawn from the cell, so the balanced potential difference equals the emf:
\(\varepsilon = K l = 5 \times 10^{-3} \times 2.16\)
\(\therefore \varepsilon = 1.080 \times 10^{-2} = 0.01080\) V
(Note the length must be converted to metres, because the potential gradient is given per metre.)

Given: resistance of the potentiometer wire \(R_w = 8\ \Omega\), its length \(L = 8\) m, battery emf \(\varepsilon = 2\) V, required potential gradient \(K = 1\ \mu\)V/mm.
First convert the required gradient to SI units:
\(K = \dfrac{1 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{V}}{1 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}} = 1 \times 10^{-3}\) V/m
Potential difference required across the whole wire:
\(V_w = K L = 1 \times 10^{-3} \times 8 = 8 \times 10^{-3}\) V
Current that must flow through the wire:
\(I = \dfrac{V_w}{R_w} = \dfrac{8 \times 10^{-3}}{8} = 1 \times 10^{-3}\) A
The battery drives this current through the series combination of the resistance box \(R_b\) and the wire (the internal resistance of the battery is not given, so it is neglected):
\(R_{total} = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{I} = \dfrac{2}{1 \times 10^{-3}} = 2000\ \Omega\)
\(\therefore R_b = R_{total} - R_w = 2000 - 8\)
\(\therefore R_b = 1992\ \Omega\)

Each resistor is \(10\ \Omega\). Reading the network off the figure, there are seven resistors: F-G, G-A, A-B, G-H, H-B, H-K and K-F, where K is the corner at which the lowest horizontal resistor meets the lower right vertical resistor. The wire E-F carries no resistor, so E and F are the same point; likewise B, C and D are joined by plain wire and are the same point.
Simplify the two chains that pass through a two-terminal node:
G to B through A: \(10 + 10 = 20\ \Omega\)
F to H through K: \(10 + 10 = 20\ \Omega\)
So between F and B the network reduces to four nodes F, G, H, B with
F-G \(= 10\ \Omega\), G-B \(= 20\ \Omega\), F-H \(= 20\ \Omega\), H-B \(= 10\ \Omega\), and the bridge arm G-H \(= 10\ \Omega\).
This is a Wheatstone bridge with F and B as the supply terminals and G-H as the galvanometer arm. It is NOT balanced, because
\(\dfrac{\text{FG}}{\text{GB}} = \dfrac{10}{20} = \dfrac{1}{2}\) while \(\dfrac{\text{FH}}{\text{HB}} = \dfrac{20}{10} = 2\)
so current does flow through G-H and a simple series-parallel reduction is not possible. Solve by Kirchhoff's laws instead.
Take \(V_F = 0\) and \(V_B = V\), and apply the junction law at G and at H.
At G: \(\dfrac{V_G}{10} + \dfrac{V_G - V}{20} + \dfrac{V_G - V_H}{10} = 0\), which gives \(5 V_G - 2 V_H = V\).
At H: \(\dfrac{V_H}{20} + \dfrac{V_H - V}{10} + \dfrac{V_H - V_G}{10} = 0\), which gives \(5 V_H - 2 V_G = 2V\).
Solving the two equations: \(V_H = \dfrac{4V}{7}\) and \(V_G = \dfrac{3V}{7}\).
The total current entering at B and leaving at F is the sum of the currents arriving at F:
\(I = \dfrac{V_G - 0}{10} + \dfrac{V_H - 0}{20} = \dfrac{3V}{70} + \dfrac{4V}{140} = \dfrac{5V}{70} = \dfrac{V}{14}\)
\(\therefore R_{FB} = \dfrac{V}{I} = 14\ \Omega\)

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed answer is 1.66 V. The exact value is \(V = \dfrac{2}{120} \times 100 = \dfrac{5}{3} = 1.6667\) V, so to two decimal places it is 1.67 V, not 1.66 V — the book has truncated rather than rounded. The physics and the method are otherwise correct.]

Given: voltmeter resistance \(R_V = 100\ \Omega\), emf \(\varepsilon = 2\) V, internal resistance \(r = 20\ \Omega\).
The voltmeter is connected across the cell, so
\(I = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{R_V + r} = \dfrac{2}{100 + 20} = \dfrac{2}{120} = \dfrac{1}{60}\) A
The voltmeter reads the terminal potential difference:
\(V = I R_V = \dfrac{1}{60} \times 100 = \dfrac{5}{3}\)
\(\therefore V = 1.67\) V (to two decimal places)
Again the reading is less than the emf of 2 V, because the voltmeter draws a current of \(1/60\) A from the cell.
